levels.title: Think Before You Prompt
levels.goal: Understand a problem well enough to explain it before asking anyone, human or AI, for help.

steps.title: Restate the problem in your own words
steps.why: Most wrong answers start with a misread question. If you can't restate the problem, you can't judge whether an AI answer solves it.

activity.task: Pick any LeetCode Easy problem you haven't solved. Without coding, write: (1) the problem in one sentence, (2) the inputs and outputs with types, (3) one example worked by hand.
activity.deliverable: A 5-8 line problem summary you could hand to a friend.

tryFirst: Read the problem twice, slowly
Underline every constraint (sizes, ranges, edge cases)
Work one example by hand on paper
reflect: Did the AI's rephrasing notice anything you missed?
Which constraint would have changed your approach if you'd ignored it?

steps.title: Write test cases before solutions
steps.why: Examples are how you check understanding. Writing them first means you have a way to verify any solution, including one an AI writes.

activity.task: For the same problem, write 6 test cases: 2 normal, 2 edge (empty, single element, max size), 2 tricky (duplicates, negatives, unsorted).
activity.deliverable: A table of input → expected output with one line on why each case matters.

tryFirst: Ask: what's the smallest input? the largest?
Ask: what input would break a naive solution?
Compute every expected output by hand
reflect: Which test cases did the AI add that you didn't think of?
Did any of your expected outputs turn out to be wrong?

steps.title: Surface your assumptions
steps.why: 90% of wrong answers come from wrong assumptions, not wrong reasoning. Juniors assume silently; seniors say their assumptions out loud.

activity.task: Take a vague college-project requirement (e.g. "build a login page"). List every assumption you'd have to make, and mark each Safe / Risky / Unknown.
activity.deliverable: An assumption table and 3 questions you'd ask before building.

tryFirst: List at least 8 assumptions on your own
Mark which ones would cause rework if wrong
Turn the Unknowns into questions
reflect: Which assumption would have cost you the most time if you'd guessed wrong?
How many of the AI's assumptions were ones you'd never have questioned?

steps.title: Find the principle behind the problem
steps.why: Problems that look new usually belong to a family you already know. Naming the family turns one problem into a reusable skill.

activity.task: Pick 3 problems you've solved before. For each, name the underlying principle or pattern (e.g. two pointers, hashing for lookup, BFS for shortest path) and one other problem it solves.
activity.deliverable: A 3-row table: problem → principle → another problem it applies to.

tryFirst: Ask: what is this problem really about?
Recall a similar problem you've seen
Name the pattern before looking anything up
reflect: Did the AI name a more general principle than you did?
Where else could you use this pattern this week?

levels.title: Break It Down
levels.goal: Split big tasks into small, ordered steps you can finish and check one at a time.

steps.title: Decompose into sub-problems
steps.why: Large problems feel impossible because you're holding all of them at once. Small pieces are each easy, and the order between them is the real plan.

activity.task: Take a feature like "users can reset their password by email". Break it into the smallest sub-problems you can, ordered so each builds on the last.
activity.deliverable: A numbered list of 6-12 sub-problems, each finishable in under an hour.

tryFirst: Write the end state first, then work backwards
Keep splitting until each piece takes under an hour
Mark which pieces depend on others
reflect: Was your first split too big, too small, or in the wrong order?
Which sub-problem did the AI include that you'd have forgotten until the end?

steps.title: Plan before you code
steps.why: Ten minutes of planning saves hours of rewriting. AI is fastest when you hand it a plan, not a wish.

activity.task: For a small CRUD app of your choice (to-do list, expense tracker), write a plan: data model, list of screens or endpoints, and the order you'll build them.
activity.deliverable: A one-page plan with a build order and a definition of done for each part.

tryFirst: Sketch the data model on paper
List the endpoints or screens
Decide what 'done' means for each one
reflect: What did the AI question in your plan, and was it right?
Which part of the plan are you least sure about now?

steps.title: Compare approaches before picking one
steps.why: There is rarely one right answer. Comparing options on purpose is what turns a coder into an engineer.

activity.task: Choose a decision in your project (e.g. where to store data: localStorage, a SQL database, or Firebase). Describe 3 options and score each on effort, risk, and fit.
activity.deliverable: A small comparison table and a one-sentence decision with your reason.

tryFirst: Name 3 genuinely different options
Write one way each could go wrong
Commit to a choice before asking the AI
reflect: Did the AI pick the same option? If not, whose reasoning was stronger?
What would make you change your decision later?

steps.title: Lock your requirements
steps.why: AI (and humans) reliably satisfy most requirements and quietly drop the rest. A numbered checklist makes 'done' checkable.

activity.task: Take an assignment brief or a job-posting take-home task. Number every requirement, then check a finished solution against the list.
activity.deliverable: A numbered requirement list with ✅ or ❌ and evidence for each.

tryFirst: Extract every 'must' and 'should' yourself
Look for requirements hidden in examples
Mark conflicts between requirements
reflect: How many requirements did you miss on the first read?
Did the AI's solution actually satisfy all of them?

levels.title: Read & Understand Code
levels.goal: Read code you didn't write, including AI-generated code, and explain it accurately.

steps.title: Explain code you didn't write
steps.why: You will read far more code than you write. If you can't explain AI-generated code, you can't own it, debug it, or defend it in an interview.

activity.task: Pick a 30-60 line file from an open-source project or a classmate's repo. Write a plain-English explanation and add a comment to every block.
activity.deliverable: The commented file and a 5-sentence summary of what it does and why.

tryFirst: Read top to bottom once without stopping
Trace one input through the code by hand
Write your explanation before asking AI
reflect: What did you misunderstand that the AI explained?
What did the AI explain wrongly or vaguely?

steps.title: Trace data through a codebase
steps.why: Real bugs live between files. Following one request from button click to database is the skill that makes you useful on day one of a job.

activity.task: In any full-stack project, trace one action (e.g. 'Add to cart') from the UI event to the database write and back. Name every file and function it passes through.
activity.deliverable: A numbered trace of 6-15 hops with file:function for each.

tryFirst: Start from the UI and search for the handler
Follow imports and calls, writing each hop down
Note where data changes shape
reflect: Which hop was hardest to find, and how did you find it?
Did the AI's map of the codebase match your trace?

steps.title: Learn one concept deeply
steps.why: Interviews test whether you understand why, not whether you can recite what. One concept learned deeply beats ten skimmed.

activity.task: Pick one concept you use but can't fully explain (closures, HashMap internals, indexes, the event loop). Write your own explanation with an example and one common mistake.
activity.deliverable: A half-page explanation you could teach to a junior.

tryFirst: Write what you think it is, from memory
Build a tiny example and run it
Predict an output, then check it
reflect: What did the AI's Socratic questions expose in your understanding?
Can you now explain it without notes?

steps.title: Solve a DSA problem with a mentor, not a solver
steps.why: Copying solutions feels like progress but isn't. Using AI as a hint-giver keeps the thinking yours.

activity.task: Solve one LeetCode Medium. Use the DSA mentor prompt so the AI only gives hints. Write down each hint you needed.
activity.deliverable: Your accepted solution, its complexity, and the list of hints you used.

tryFirst: Spend at least 20 minutes before any hint
Write a brute-force solution first
State the time complexity of your approach
reflect: Which hint unlocked the problem, and could you have found it yourself?
What pattern will you recognise next time?

levels.title: Debug Like a Scientist
levels.goal: Find root causes with evidence instead of guessing, and verify AI answers before trusting them.

steps.title: Debug with hypotheses
steps.why: Random changes until it works teaches you nothing and often hides the real bug. Hypotheses make debugging fast and repeatable.

activity.task: Next time something breaks, before changing any code write: verified facts, 3 hypotheses ranked by likelihood, and what you'd expect to see if each were true. Then test the top one.
activity.deliverable: A short debugging log: facts → hypotheses → test → result.

tryFirst: Write only facts you've verified
Rank 3 possible causes
Design one check that separates them
reflect: Was your most likely hypothesis right?
What evidence would have saved you the most time?

steps.title: Read errors and logs properly
steps.why: Most error messages tell you exactly what's wrong if you read them carefully. Pasting them straight into AI skips the skill you need most.

activity.task: Collect 3 real error messages or stack traces from your projects. For each, find the line that matters, explain the error in your own words, and fix it.
activity.deliverable: 3 entries: error → the key line → your explanation → the fix.

tryFirst: Find the first line that mentions your code
Read the error type and message word by word
Search the docs before asking AI
reflect: How close was your explanation to the AI's?
Which part of a stack trace do you now read first?

steps.title: Find bugs in code that runs
steps.why: The worst bugs don't crash; they quietly do the wrong thing. Spotting them is what code reviewers and interviewers look for.

activity.task: Take a function you wrote this month. List what it should do, then hunt for cases where it doesn't: off-by-one, null inputs, wrong comparisons, missing awaits.
activity.deliverable: At least 2 bugs or risks found, each with a failing input and a fix.

tryFirst: Write the expected behaviour first
Try empty, null, and boundary inputs
Look for missing awaits and == vs ===
reflect: Did the AI find a bug you missed? What kind?
Did the AI claim a bug that wasn't real?

steps.title: Verify AI answers before trusting them
steps.why: AI states guesses with the same confidence as facts. A vibe coder ships the guess; an AI-assisted developer verifies it.

activity.task: Ask an AI a factual technical question you care about. Then verify every claim against official docs or by running code, and mark each claim correct, partly correct, or wrong.
activity.deliverable: The AI answer with each claim marked and a source or test for each.

tryFirst: Write what you believe the answer is first
Find the official docs page for the topic
Decide how you'll test each claim
reflect: How many claims were wrong or outdated?
Which kinds of questions will you always verify from now on?

levels.title: Build in Small Chunks
levels.goal: Build features in small, tested, reviewed increments: the habit that separates professionals from vibe coders.

steps.title: Write tests that catch real bugs
steps.why: Tests are how you prove code works, whoever wrote it. They're also the safety net that lets you use AI to change code without fear.

activity.task: Pick one function with real logic (validation, pricing, dates). Write tests covering happy path, edge cases, and errors before asking AI for more.
activity.deliverable: A test file with at least 6 tests, all passing.

tryFirst: Write test names first (should_X_when_Y)
Cover one edge case per input
Make one test fail on purpose to check it works
reflect: Which AI-suggested test caught something real?
Which AI-suggested test was pointless?

steps.title: Ship in small commits and PRs
steps.why: Small commits are easy to review, revert, and explain. Interviewers and teams judge you by your git history.

activity.task: Build one small feature in at least 4 commits, each doing one thing, then open a PR with a clear description.
activity.deliverable: A PR link with 4+ focused commits and a What / Why / How to test description.

tryFirst: Plan the commits before coding
Write each commit message yourself first
Describe how a reviewer should test it
reflect: How did the AI's commit messages differ from yours?
Would a reviewer understand your PR without asking you?

steps.title: Review your own code like a senior
steps.why: Catching your own mistakes before review builds trust fast. Asking AI to review is useful only if you reviewed first.

activity.task: Before your next PR, review your own diff with a checklist: bugs, security, performance, naming. Then run the AI review and compare.
activity.deliverable: Two lists, your findings and the AI's, with what you fixed.

tryFirst: Read the diff as if someone else wrote it
Check every input for validation
Look for duplicated logic
reflect: What percentage of the AI's findings had you already caught?
Which AI finding was wrong, and how did you know?

steps.title: Refactor without breaking things
steps.why: Real jobs are mostly changing existing code. Refactoring with tests in place is how you improve code without fear.

activity.task: Pick your messiest file. Make sure it has tests, then refactor one thing at a time (rename, extract function, remove duplication), running tests after each change.
activity.deliverable: A before/after diff, green tests, and one sentence per change on why it's better.

tryFirst: Get tests passing before touching anything
Change one thing, then run tests
Stop when it's clearer, not perfect
reflect: Did any AI refactor change behaviour? Did your tests catch it?
Which change made the biggest difference to readability?

levels.title: Ship & Get Job-Ready
levels.goal: Deploy, document, and explain your work so recruiters and interviewers can see what you can do.

steps.title: Deploy a project for real
steps.why: A live link beats a GitHub repo nobody runs. Deploying teaches environment config, secrets, and builds, all things you'll do at work.

activity.task: Deploy one of your projects to a free host with automatic deploys from your main branch. Add a health check or status page.
activity.deliverable: A live URL and a short note on how deploys work.

tryFirst: Read your host's quick-start docs
List the environment variables your app needs
Try a manual deploy before automating it
reflect: What broke during deployment that never broke locally?
Which part of the AI's pipeline did you have to fix?

steps.title: Document your project
steps.why: Clear docs show you understand your own work. A good README is the first thing a recruiter reads.

activity.task: Write a README for your deployed project: what it does, screenshot, tech stack, how to run it, and one design decision you're proud of.
activity.deliverable: A README a stranger could follow to run your project in 10 minutes.

tryFirst: Write the README before asking AI
Ask a friend to follow it and note where they get stuck
Explain one decision in your own words
reflect: What did the AI's critique say was missing?
Did your friend get stuck somewhere the AI didn't predict?

steps.title: Explain a system design
steps.why: Interviews for good roles ask how you'd design systems. Explaining your own project's design is the best practice you can get.

activity.task: Draw the architecture of your project (boxes and arrows), then answer: what breaks at 100x users, and how would you fix it?
activity.deliverable: A diagram and a one-page scaling plan.

tryFirst: Draw it on paper first
Find the single point of failure
Estimate requests per second at 100x
reflect: Which bottleneck did the AI spot that you missed?
Could you defend your design to a skeptical interviewer?

steps.title: Practise interviews with honest feedback
steps.why: Interviewing is a skill you can practise. Mock interviews with brutal scoring show your gaps while they're still cheap to fix.

activity.task: Run one full mock interview (DSA + design + behavioural). Answer out loud or in writing without looking anything up. Record your scores.
activity.deliverable: Your scores per section and a 2-week plan for your weakest area.

tryFirst: Answer without any notes or lookups
Time yourself like a real interview
Write your own self-score before seeing the AI's
reflect: Where did your self-score differ most from the AI's?
What is the single gap you'll close first?
